questions.question: A train departs from Station P for Station Q at 8:00 AM, traveling at a speed of 60 km/h. Another train departs from Station Q for Station P at 10:00 AM traveling at a speed of 70 km/h. The distance between the two stations is 510 km. At what time will the two trains cross each other?
questions.questionHtml: A train departs from Station P for Station Q at 8:00 AM, traveling at a speed of 60 km/h. Another train departs from Station Q for Station P at 10:00 AM traveling at a speed of 70 km/h. The distance between the two stations is 510 km. At what time will the two trains cross each other?
questions.solution:
Distance covered by Train 1 before 10:00 AM

Train 1 starts at 8:00 AM, 2 hours earlier.
Distance covered in 2 hours = 60 × 2 = 120 km

Remaining distance = 510 − 120 = 390 km

Relative speed after 10:00 AM

Both trains are moving towards each other.
Relative speed = 60 + 70 = 130 km/h

Time taken to meet after 10:00 AM

Time = Distance / Speed = 390 / 130 = 3 hours

Meeting time

10:00 AM + 3 hours = 1:00 PM

questions.question: Two individuals, A and B, have rented a field. A places 27 horses in the field for 6 months and 15 cows for 2 months. B adds 15 cows for 6 months and 40 sheep for 7.5 months. If 3 horses consume the same amount of food as 5 cows, and 6 cows eat as much as 10 sheep, what portion of the rent should A cover?
questions.questionHtml: Two individuals, A and B, have rented a field. A places 27 horses in the field for 6 months and 15 cows for 2 months. B adds 15 cows for 6 months and 40 sheep for 7.5 months. If 3 horses consume the same amount of food as 5 cows, and 6 cows eat as much as 10 sheep, what portion of the rent should A cover?
questions.solution:
Given relations

Convert everything into cow units

For A:

A keeps
→ 27 horses for 6 months
→ 15 cows for 2 months

So,
Horse part = 27 × (5/3) × 6 = 27 × 10 = 270 cow-months
Cow part = 15 × 2 = 30 cow-months

Total for A = 270 + 30 = 300 cow-months

For B:

B keeps
→ 15 cows for 6 months
→ 40 sheep for 7.5 months

Now, 6 cows = 10 sheep ⇒ 1 sheep = 3/5 cow

So,
Cow part = 15 × 6 = 90 cow-months
Sheep part = 40 × (3/5) × 7.5 = 40 × 4.5 = 180 cow-months

Total for B = 90 + 180 = 270 cow-months

Ratio of rent

A : B = 300 : 270 = 10 : 9

Hence, A’s share = 10 / (10 + 9) = 10/19

questions.question: If the average of N consecutive numbers is 25, find the average of N + 4 consecutive numbers.
questions.questionHtml: If the average of N consecutive numbers is 25, find the average of N + 4 consecutive numbers.
questions.solution:
Let N = 3 consecutive numbers → 24, 25, 26
Their average = (24 + 25 + 26) / 3 = 25

Now, take N + 4 = 7 consecutive numbers → 24, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30
Their average = (24 + 30) / 2 = 27

✅ So, the new average = 27

questions.question: Mukesh sells two shirts. The cost price (CP) of the first shirt = selling price (SP) of the second shirt. The first shirt is sold at 20% profit, and the second at 20% loss. Find the ratio of selling price of the first to the cost price of the second.
questions.questionHtml: Mukesh sells two shirts. The cost price (CP) of the first shirt = selling price (SP) of the second shirt. The first shirt is sold at 20% profit, and the second at 20% loss. Find the ratio of selling price of the first to the cost price of the second.
questions.solution:
Let the cost price of the first shirt = ₹100
Then, selling price of the first shirt = 100 + 20% of 100 = ₹120

Now,
Given that cost price of first = selling price of second,
So, SP₂ = ₹100

The second shirt is sold at 20% loss,
Let cost price of the second = x
Then, SP₂ = x × (1 − 20/100) = 0.8x

⇒ 0.8x = 100
⇒ x = 100 / 0.8 = ₹125

Now ratio:

SP₁ : CP₂ = 120 : 125 = 24 : 25

questions.questionHtml: How many numbers between 400 and 700 are divisible by 5, 6, and 7?
questions.solution:
A number divisible by 5, 6, and 7 must be divisible by their LCM.

LCM of 5, 6, and 7 = 210

Now find multiples of 210 between 400 and 700:

210 × 1 = 210 (less than 400)
210 × 2 = 420 ✅
210 × 3 = 630 ✅
210 × 4 = 840 (greater than 700)

So, only 420 and 630 lie between 400 and 700.

questions.question: The price of an article increased by 33.33% every year. If the difference between the prices at the end of fourth year and fifth year is ₹144, then find the price at the end of the second year.
questions.questionHtml:
The price of an article increased by 33.33% every year.
If the difference between the prices at the end of fourth year and fifth year is ₹144, then find the price at the end of the second year.
questions.solution:
33.33% = 1/3

2nd → 3rd → 4th → 5th

At 33.33% increase every year → multiply by 4/3 each time.

Given:
Difference between 4th and 5th year = 144
⇒ 1 part = 144
⇒ 3 parts = 144 × 3 = 432 (price at end of 4th year)

Now going backward:
4th → 3rd → 2nd

= 144 × 3 × (3/4) × (3/4)
= 144 × (3³) / (4²)
= 144 × 27 / 16 = 243

Odds against drawing a Club = non-Clubs : Clubs = 39 : 13 = 3 : 1

Read both the statements and select the most appropriate answer. Five friends X, Y, Z, A, and B are of different ages. How many of them are older than B? (I) Only Z is older than Y. X is older than A. (II) Exactly two people are younger than X. B is older than A, but younger than X.
questions.questionHtml:
A question is followed by two statements numbered I and II. You have to decide whether the data provided in the statements are sufficient to answer the question. Read both the statements and select the most appropriate answer.
Five friends X, Y, Z, A, and B are of different ages. How many of them are older than B?
(I) Only Z is older than Y. X is older than A.
(II) Exactly two people are younger than X. B is older than A, but younger than X.

options.text: Both statements I and II together are NOT sufficient to answer the question
options.html: Both statements I and II together are NOT sufficient to answer the question

options.text: Data in Statement I alone is sufficient to answer the question while data in statement II is not
options.html: Data in Statement I alone is sufficient to answer the question while data in statement II is not

options.text: Both statements I and II together (and not statement I alone or statement II alone) are sufficient to answer the question
options.html: Both statements I and II together (and not statement I alone or statement II alone) are sufficient to answer the question

options.text: Data in Statement II alone is sufficient to answer the question while data in statement I is not
options.html: Data in Statement II alone is sufficient to answer the question while data in statement I is not

questions.solution:
Answer: Data in Statement II alone is sufficient while Statement I is not.

Why:

Statement I:
“Only Z is older than Y” ⇒ Y is 2nd oldest; “X older than A” ⇒ X > A.
No info about B’s position ⇒ not sufficient.

Statement II:
“Exactly two people are younger than X” ⇒ X is 3rd (two above, two below).
“B is older than A, but younger than X” ⇒ Order fixes as: (Y, Z) > X > B > A.
Thus, people older than B are Y, Z, X ⇒ 3.
This is uniquely determined ⇒ sufficient.

questions.question: Eight students A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are standing in a row in a decreasing order of their heights but not necessarily in the same order. E is taller than B but shorter than C. H is taller than G and D. Only one person is shorter than D. As many persons are taller than A as many persons are shorter than F. A is taller than C who is taller than H. B is not just taller than D. E is shorter than H but taller than G. Question: How many persons are taller than E?

Eight students A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H are standing in a row in a decreasing order of their heights but not necessarily in the same order.
E is taller than B but shorter than C.
H is taller than G and D.

As many persons are taller than A as many persons are shorter than F.

B is not just taller than D.
E is shorter than H but taller than G.
Question: How many persons are taller than E?
questions.solution:
Arrange all students by height (top to bottom):
A > C > H > E > G > B > D > F

questions.question: Given below is a statement (Cause) followed by possible effects numbered I, II, and III. Read the ‘Cause’ carefully and decide which of the three can be possible effect(s). Cause: Many students in City Y reported receiving incorrect exam schedules this week. Possible Effects: I. The Education Board has issued a corrected schedule and notified all students. II. The city administration clarified that a technical error in the database caused the wrong schedules. III. Long queues of students were seen outside the university offices to get the corrected schedules.
questions.questionHtml:
Given below is a statement (Cause) followed by possible effects numbered I, II, and III. Read the ‘Cause’ carefully and decide which of the three can be possible effect(s).
Cause:
Many students in City Y reported receiving incorrect exam schedules this week.
Possible Effects:
I. The Education Board has issued a corrected schedule and notified all students.
II. The city administration clarified that a technical error in the database caused the wrong schedules.
III. Long queues of students were seen outside the university offices to get the corrected schedules.

options.text: Only II is a possible effect
Both I and II are possible effects
options.html: Both I and II are possible effects

options.text: Only I is a possible effect
Both II and III are possible effects
options.html: Both II and III are possible effects

questions.solution:
The correct answer is: Both II and III are possible effects
Here's why:
Effect II is plausible because when errors like incorrect exam schedules occur, it's common for the administration to investigate and issue a clarification. A technical error in the database is a reasonable explanation.
Effect III is also likely, as students would naturally seek clarification or corrected schedules in person, leading to long queues at university offices.
Effect I, while possible, assumes that the Education Board has already acted and notified all students. This is more of a resolution than an immediate effect and may not occur in every case.
So, the most reasonable choice is: Both II and III are possible effects.
